previous_description: A behavior element that groups behavior based on required capabilities, skills, or resources (e.g., HR management, financial reporting). Unlike BusinessProcess, it is not goal-oriented but competency-oriented.
definition: A business behavior element that groups ongoing internal behavior by the competency, skill, knowledge or resource it requires (e.g. Accounting, Claims Handling, Procurement), performed by a BusinessRole or BusinessActor, with no defined start, end or ordered sequence of steps.

distinguish_from.when: the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a trigger and a defined end result (e.g. 'Handle Insurance Claim from submission to payout') rather than a standing area of competence.
the element describes externally visible behavior from the consumer's perspective (what is offered), rather than the internal grouping of work that realizes it.
the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles in a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor.
the element names who holds responsibility (e.g. 'Claims Handler', 'Finance Department') rather than the behavior they perform (e.g. 'Claims Handling', 'Financial Accounting').

code_evidence: top-level packages, modules or bounded contexts named after organizational competency areas (e.g. billing/, hr/, accounting/, procurement/) that own many related workflows rather than a single one

CODEOWNERS, team-ownership or service-catalog entries mapping a department or functional team to a group of modules, or permission scopes/menu sections grouped by functional area (e.g. 'finance:*', a 'Human Resources' navigation section)

architecture docs, capability or function maps, or ADRs listing functional areas of the business (e.g. a 'Business Functions' table or level-1 functional decomposition) referenced by code comments or module READMEs

attribute_descriptions.name: documentation
attribute_descriptions.description: Free-text description of the competency area this function covers, its scope boundaries and the roles that perform it; set whenever the name alone does not make the grouped behavior unambiguous.

notes: BusinessInteraction's definition says functions are 'performed by an actor' while this layer's relationships use roles; align wording. 'realizes motivation.goal' contradicts 'not goal-oriented'; ArchiMate core elements realize requirements and influence goals. 'serves businessrole' is unusual for a function. The capability-vs-function boundary with product.capability needs explicit guidance.
